findings.title: Local cache is populated before the device-limit check, letting rejected devices bypass the limit
findings.body: In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` runs before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)`. Now that client.go treats `ErrDeviceLimitReached` as an authentication failure, this ordering breaks enforcement: when a new device is rejected because the limit is reached, its cache key has already been set, so every subsequent request from that same device for the next ~29 minutes hits the cache branch, returns nil from TagDevice, and is allowed to authenticate anonymously. The device limit is therefore only enforced on the first request from each new device, not on ongoing usage. The cache should only be populated after the store call succeeds (or the error should clear the key).

findings.title: Count-then-insert device limit check is not atomic and can be exceeded under concurrency
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first running CountDevices and then, if under the limit, executing the upsert in a separate statement without a transaction or lock. Multiple concurrent anonymous requests with fresh device IDs can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, pushing the total above the configured limit. On a busy instance with many simultaneous first-time anonymous hits, the actual number of tracked devices can significantly exceed the configured limit. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g. a transaction with appropriate isolation, a conditional INSERT based on a subquery count, or a database constraint).

findings.title: Devices idle longer than 30 days are permanently locked out when the limit is reached
findings.body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at falls between device.UpdatedAt-30d and device.UpdatedAt+1min, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached if no row matched. However, old devices are only physically deleted after 61 days (keepFor in impl.go). A device that was tagged 31-60 days ago still exists in anon_device but is neither counted by CountDevices (which uses the same 30-day window) nor updatable by updateDevice, so on an at-limit instance that returning device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and is denied authentication even though it already occupies a row and could simply be refreshed. The 30-day exclusion window in updateDevice should be widened (or removed) so any existing device row can be updated.

findings.title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned as a raw error, producing a 500 for anonymous users
findings.body: When the device limit is reached, Authenticate returns the plain `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` error. The authn framework will treat this as a generic internal authentication error (HTTP 500 with 'device limit reached') rather than a deliberate access-denied response, making it indistinguishable from a server failure in monitoring and giving end users a confusing error. Consider returning a typed error (e.g. one the authn layer maps to 401/403 with a clear message) so operators and users can tell the limit was hit.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as possibly-undefined but backend always sends a number
findings.body: The Go DTO serializes `anonymousDeviceLimit` as a non-omitempty int64, so the frontend always receives a number — 0 meaning 'no limit'. The TypeScript type `number | undefined` suggests the field can be absent, which can lead frontend consumers to use undefined-checks to detect 'no limit configured' and misbehave, since the actual sentinel is 0 and the value will never be undefined. Type it as `number` and document 0 as unlimited (or make the Go field a pointer with omitempty if undefined is intended).
